I will keep my land in the standard Quzhou pattern: winter wheat first, then summer maize on the same fields. I am in southern Hebei on the North China Plain, and this wheat-maize double-cropping system is still the main local system, so I would not switch to something riskier this year. It fits our climate, our machinery, and the way water comes here: wheat needs the more careful irrigation management, while maize can use the summer rains better.

Because my exact farm size was not given, I will make this plan for 20 mu of land. I will plant improved winter wheat in autumn and then hybrid summer maize right after wheat harvest. For wheat, I will not chase the very highest demonstration-field yield, because that usually needs tighter management and sometimes more cost. I will aim for steady production with moderate fertilizer, two irrigations as the base plan, and two pesticide sprays. For maize, I will use no-tillage sowing into wheat stubble, because that is practical in this system and saves time after harvest. I will keep fertilizer moderate, depend mainly on rainfall, and only irrigate once if summer drought shows up. My goal is stable grain output, controlled input cost, and less pressure on groundwater.

I’m basing these choices on current Quzhou and North China Plain sources showing that Quzhou is still dominated by winter wheat-summer maize rotation, that most rainfall comes during the maize season, that local “green ton-and-a-half grain” work in Quzhou is centered on wheat-maize with water and fertilizer reduction, and on official fertilizer guidance for Hebei/southern North China wheat and maize:
